newsitem.title: FRANCE: Strike disrupts French train traffic.
newsitem.headline: Strike disrupts French train traffic.

text.p: A 36-hour strike against plans to reform state railways disrupted train traffic unevenly across France on Thursday and more social unrest loomed as civil service trade unions threatened to strike for higher wages.
The SNCF state railway company said 30 percent of staff stopped work, cutting main line traffic by one to two-thirds.
Despite the protest and left-wing opposition, a National Assembly committee passed government plans to split the heavily indebted SNCF in two as part of efforts to bolster its finances.
The plans, already approved in the Senate (upper house), will go to full debate in the assembly next Tuesday.
The rail protest was due to end at 8 a.m. (0700 GMT) on Friday. It began cutting into services at around 8 p.m. (1900 GMT) on Wednesday.
SNCF said Eurostar trains through the Channel Tunnel between Paris and London ran normally, and high-speed Thalys trains to Brussels were hardly affected.
Other high-speed rail traffic was cut by one third to one half. Service on conventional main and regional lines was between 25 and 65 percent of normal, with the southeast worst affected.
Commuter traffic in the Paris region was also hit.
While SNCF said the percentage of strikers was much lower than in previous stoppages last October and in 1995, when a strike by rail workers crippled the country for several weeks.
Denis Andlauer, head of the CFDT rail union, said most train drivers stopped work, but he acknowledged the strike call may have been blunted by the complexity of the issues involved.

Transport Minister Bernard Pons proposes to create a state holding company to take over two-thirds of the 200 billion franc ($36 billion) debt run up by SNCF mainly in developing the high-speed TGV train system.
The holding company would own the rail network and charge SNCF for using it.
The Communist-led CGT and Socialist CFDT unions, with a majority of the 180,000 rail staff, say the legislation will break up SNCF, threatening the rail monopoly, jobs and loss-making railway lines.
More social unrest loomed as civil service unions said they would discuss calling a strike after the government announces pay offers next Tuesday.

CGC union leader Pierre Avignon said unofficial contacts with the civil service ministry in the past few days led unions to believe the government was not willing to make any concessions on a "catch-up" after a wage freeze in 1996.
Turnout in the last strike on October 17, to protest against planned job cuts, was relatively modest with one in three civil servants stopping work.

A public transport protest in the southwestern town of Toulouse went into its fourth day, with bus and tram drivers striking to press demands for a cut in working hours, early retirement at 55 instead of 60, and safer working conditions.
Strikers blocked access to the city's two bus depots. They voted to extend the stoppage for another 24 hours to Friday.
